title: Atrial fibrillation
summary: Sinus rhythm, and then the atria start to fibrillate.
description: In atrial fibrillation the atria do not contract together: there are no P waves, and impulses reach the ventricles at irregular intervals, so the R–R intervals vary without any pattern (the small, fast fibrillation waves that take the place of the P waves are often too small to see, as here). This excerpt of an ambulatory ECG begins in sinus rhythm: a small P wave before each QRS (zoom in to see it; it is clearest in ECG 2) and nearly equal R–R intervals. After about 28 seconds the atria start to fibrillate, and the ventricles beat faster and irregularly. The strip at the top names the rhythm as the database marks it (it marks atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter and junctional rhythm, and calls the rest 'other rhythms': here sinus rhythm, as the P waves and the regular beats show).
look_for: The R–R intervals: nearly equal in sinus rhythm, varying without any pattern once the fibrillation starts (measure a few of each)
A small P wave before each QRS in sinus rhythm (zoom in; it is clearest in ECG 2), and none during the fibrillation
The rate of the ventricles before and during the fibrillation (switch on the heart rate)

channels.name: ECG 1

channels.name: ECG 2

beats.note: The beats were found automatically by the workbench (the R waves of ECG 1) and checked by eye, and against the database's own beat marks (which a program made, and nobody checked); they are not labelled.

subject.notes: One of 25 people with atrial fibrillation, mostly paroxysmal (it comes and goes), whose 10-hour ambulatory ECGs make up the database; their age and sex are not given.
